title: GTNW - U.S. offensive options by era (1789-2030)
scope_note: Encyclopedia-level game-design research. Dates are first/last year available to the U.S.; 'approx' and 'UNCERTAIN' flags mark estimates. No technical weapon details.

status_legend.legal: No binding legal bar on possession/use beyond general law of war
status_legend.restricted: Lawful but limited by treaty caps, ratified use-bans with reservations, statute or binding policy
status_legend.treaty_banned: Possession/use banned by a treaty the U.S. is party to

eras.name: Early republic, Quasi-War, Barbary Wars, War of 1812
key_facts: No navy at all until 1797: the Continental Navy was disbanded in 1785; the Naval Act of 1794 funded six frigates (first launched 1797); Navy Department created 30 Apr 1798.
Army: ~700-840 regulars in 1789; Legion of the United States 1792-96; War of 1812 regulars authorized ~35,000 plus state militia (often unwilling to fight outside their states).
Main offensive tools: frigates and sloops (single-ship actions), privateers, a small Marine Corps (1798), embargo (1807-09), and invasion of Canada (failed 1812-14).
Wars: Northwest Indian War (1785-95), Quasi-War with France (1798-1800, undeclared), First Barbary War (1801-05), War of 1812 (1812-15), Second Barbary War (1815).
Constraint: Congress declares war and grants letters of marque; the President cannot raise forces without appropriations.

eras.name: Distant-station squadrons, Mexican War
key_facts: Navy organized as regional squadrons (Mediterranean, West India, Pacific, Brazil, East India, Home, Africa) - see fleets list.
Ships of the line built (Act of 1816) but never fought a fleet battle. Steam enters (USS Fulton 1837, USS Princeton 1843).
Army: ~6,000-16,000 regulars; Mexican War (1846-48) ~100,000 served incl. volunteers; Scott's Veracruz landing (Mar 1847, ~10,000 men) was the first large U.S. amphibious operation.
Gunboat diplomacy: Perry opens Japan (1853-54); punitive raids (Sumatra 1832, Barrier Forts China 1856, Fiji 1855/1859).
Indian removals and wars (Seminole Wars 1816-58) are the bulk of Army combat.

eras.name: Civil War
key_facts: Union Army ~1 million at peak (1865); ~2.1M served. Conscription from 1863.
Navy grows from ~42 commissioned ships to ~670 vessels; ironclads (Monitor, Mar 1862); Anaconda blockade proclaimed 19 Apr 1861.
First U.S. air arm: Union Army Balloon Corps (1861-Aug 1863) for observation only.
Total-war methods: Sherman's march (1864), Sheridan in the Shenandoah. Lieber Code (1863) - first codified U.S. law-of-war instructions.
GAME NOTE: largely an internal war; foreign-attack options limited by need to keep Britain/France neutral (Trent Affair 1861).

eras.name: Reconstruction, Indian Wars, the 'New Navy'
key_facts: Army capped at ~25,000 enlisted (1876); fighting on the Plains (Little Bighorn 1876, Wounded Knee 1890).

Navy decays post-war to a few dozen obsolete ships (often described as smaller than Chile's in 1880s - approx.), then rebuilds: ABCD steel ships authorized 1883; Naval War College 1884; Mahan's 'Influence of Sea Power' 1890; first battleships commissioned 1895.
Squadrons: European, North Atlantic, South Atlantic, Pacific, Asiatic (1868).
Overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy (1893) aided by Marines from USS Boston.

eras.name: Spanish-American War and imperial era
key_facts: Spanish-American War (Apr-Aug 1898): Dewey's Asiatic Squadron at Manila Bay (1 May), Sampson/Schley at Santiago (3 Jul); Army expands to ~275,000 incl. volunteers.
Philippine-American War (1899-1902, insurgency to ~1913); Boxer Relief (1900, ~2,500 U.S. troops); Banana Wars begin (Panama 1903, Cuba 1906, Nicaragua 1912).
Great White Fleet (16 battleships, Dec 1907-Feb 1909); first dreadnoughts commissioned 1910; first submarine USS Holland (1900); Army buys first airplane 1909, Navy 1911.
Roosevelt Corollary (1904) frames the Caribbean as a U.S. police zone.

eras.name: WWI (U.S. belligerent Apr 1917-Nov 1918)
key_facts: Veracruz occupation (1914) and Punitive Expedition into Mexico (1916-17, ~10,000 troops, 1st Aero Squadron).
Army ~4 million mobilized; AEF ~2 million in France; first U.S. tanks (Tank Corps, Renault FT) and Air Service (~45 front-line squadrons by Nov 1918).

CHEMICAL: AEF Gas Service (Aug 1917), Chemical Warfare Service (28 Jun 1918), 1st Gas Regiment; U.S. forces used gas in 1918 (legal - no ratified ban then). U.S. suffered ~70,000 gas casualties (approx.).
Navy: Battleship Division Nine with the British Grand Fleet; convoy escort; North Sea Mine Barrage (1918).
Economic: Trading with the Enemy Act (Oct 1917).

eras.name: Interwar
key_facts: Naval arms control: Washington Treaty (1922) and London Treaties (1930, 1936) cap battleships/carriers. First carrier USS Langley 1922; Lexington/Saratoga 1927.
Geneva Protocol signed 1925 but not ratified (Senate) until 1975 - chemical stockpile retained. Kellogg-Briand (1928). Neutrality Acts (1935-37) restrict arms sales to belligerents.
Army small (~120,000-190,000); Marines fight Banana Wars to 1934 (Nicaragua, Haiti); Fleet Marine Force 1933 and amphibious doctrine 1934.
Air Corps (1926) develops strategic bombing doctrine; B-17 enters service 1938. Good Neighbor Policy (1933) ends Caribbean interventions.

eras.name: WWII (U.S. belligerent Dec 1941-Sept 1945)
key_facts: Pre-war economic warfare: export controls on Japan from Jul 1940, asset freeze 26 Jul 1941, de facto oil embargo Aug 1941; Lend-Lease (Mar 1941); undeclared naval war in the Atlantic (1941).
Peak ~12 million in uniform (1945); 16 million served. Navy: 6,768 ships of all types by Aug 1945 (NHHC force levels); numbered fleets created 15 Mar 1943.
New options: carriers as capital ships, strategic bombing, airborne divisions, Rangers, OSS (13 Jun 1942), unrestricted submarine warfare, radio-guided bombs (Azon 1944), helicopters (1944).
NUCLEAR: Manhattan Project; Trinity 16 Jul 1945; Hiroshima 6 Aug, Nagasaki 9 Aug 1945. Stockpile at end of 1945: 2 (DOE).
CHEMICAL: large stockpile, FDR no-first-use pledge (Jun 1943), never used in combat. BIOLOGICAL: offensive program begins 1943 at Camp Detrick.

eras.name: Early Cold War
key_facts: National Security Act 1947: Air Force, CIA (18 Sept 1947), NSC. Strategic Air Command (1946). Covert ops authorized by NSC 10/2 (1948): Iran 1953, Guatemala 1954, Bay of Pigs 1961.
Nuclear stockpile: 299 (1950) -> 2,422 (1955) -> 18,638 (1960) -> 22,229 (1961). Thermonuclear test Ivy Mike 1952; Soviet first test 1949 ends U.S. monopoly.
Delivery: B-36, B-47, B-52 (1955); Atlas ICBM on alert Sept 1959; first Polaris SSBN patrol 15 Nov 1960; Regulus, Matador, Snark cruise missiles; Thor/Jupiter IRBMs in UK/Italy/Turkey.
Korea (1950-53) under UN mandate; massive retaliation doctrine (1954). Supercarrier Forrestal (1955); USS Nautilus (1955); USS Enterprise CVN-65 (1961).
Special Forces (1952); helicopters in Korea. Chemical: sarin production 1950s. Bio: production at Pine Bluff from 1954. First ASAT test (Bold Orion, Oct 1959).

eras.name: Vietnam era
key_facts: Cuban Missile Crisis (Oct 1962): quarantine, SAC at DEFCON 2, Jupiter withdrawal deal. Stockpile peaks at 31,255 (1967).
Triad matures: 1,054 ICBMs and 41 SSBNs by 1967; Minuteman III (1970, MIRV), Poseidon (1971).

Vietnam: peak 543,400 troops (Apr 1969); Rolling Thunder (1965-68), Arc Light B-52s, Linebacker I/II (1972, laser-guided bombs); airmobile 1st Cavalry Division; herbicides (Ranch Hand 1962-71); recon drones (1964-75); Haiphong mining (1972).

Arms control: LTBT 1963, Outer Space Treaty 1967, NPT 1970, SALT I and ABM Treaty 1972. Nixon renounces biological weapons and chemical first use (25 Nov 1969). Geneva Protocol and BWC ratified Jan 1975.
Constraints: War Powers Resolution (Nov 1973) - 60/90-day clock; Church Committee (1975); draft ends 1973. Mayaguez incident (May 1975). ASAT: Program 437 Thor (to 1975).

eras.name: Late Cold War
key_facts: Stockpile ~24,000 (1980) -> 22,217 (1989) -> 19,008 (1991). New systems: ALCM (1982), Tomahawk (1983), GLCM and Pershing II in Europe (1983), Peacekeeper (1986), B-1B (1986), Trident I (1979) and II (1990), Ohio SSBNs (1981+), secret F-117 (1983).

Treaties: SALT II (1979, unratified, observed to 1986); INF (1987, in force 1988) eliminates intermediate missiles; START I signed 31 Jul 1991. Sept 1991 Presidential Nuclear Initiatives withdraw most tactical nukes.

Ops: Desert One (1980, failed), Lebanon (1982-84), Grenada (1983), Libya El Dorado Canyon (1986), Tanker War/Praying Mantis (1988), Panama (1989), Gulf War (1991, ~540,000 deployed, first Tomahawk combat).
Delta Force (1977), SOCOM (1987), Goldwater-Nichols (1986). Navy peaks near 594 ships (1987) under the 600-ship goal.
Chemical binary production 1987-90; May 1991 U.S. forswears all chemical use. ASAT: F-15 ASM-135 kills Solwind satellite (Sept 1985). EO 12333 (1981) bans assassination; Iran-Contra (1986).

eras.name: Post-Cold War (to 10 Sept 2001)
key_facts: Stockpile 13,708 (1992) -> 10,526 (2001). Last U.S. nuclear test 23 Sept 1992; CTBT signed 1996, rejected by Senate 1999. START I in force 1994; START II never in force.

Ops: Somalia (1992-94), Haiti (1994), Bosnia Deliberate Force (1995), Iraq no-fly zones and Desert Fox (1998), Infinite Reach cruise-missile strikes on Sudan/Afghanistan (Aug 1998), Kosovo Allied Force (1999; B-2 and JDAM debut).
Predator UAV first deployed (Bosnia 1995, unarmed). Fifth Fleet re-established (1995). CWC ratified (Apr 1997) - chemical destruction begins in earnest.
Sanctions era: Iraq (1990-2003), Iran-Libya Sanctions Act (1996).

eras.name: Global War on Terror
key_facts: AUMF (18 Sept 2001) and Iraq AUMF (2002). Afghanistan (from 7 Oct 2001), Iraq (from 20 Mar 2003; ~170,000 peak 2007). Armed drones: first Predator strikes Oct 2001; targeted killing in Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia.
Stockpile 10,526 (2001) -> 4,717 (2014). Treaties: ABM withdrawal (2002), SORT (2003-11), New START (signed 8 Apr 2010, in force 5 Feb 2011). Peacekeeper retired 2005.
Cyber: Stuxnet/Olympic Games (~2007-10, attributed); USCYBERCOM (2010); Fleet Cyber Command/10th Fleet (2010). Space: Burnt Frost ASAT shot (21 Feb 2008).

SSGN conversions (2006-08); F-22 (2005); MQ-9 Reaper (2007); Fourth Fleet re-established (2008). Libya (2011, under UNSC 1973); bin Laden raid (2 May 2011); Inherent Resolve vs ISIS (from Aug 2014); Russia sanctions over Crimea (2014).

eras.name: Great-power competition (to present, Oct 2026)
key_facts: Stockpile 4,571 (2015) -> 3,748 (Sept 2023, last official figure); FAS Jan 2025: ~3,700 stockpiled, ~1,770 deployed. W76-2 low-yield SLBM warhead deployed (2019).

Treaties: INF withdrawal (2 Aug 2019); Russia suspends New START participation (Feb 2023); New START EXPIRED 5 Feb 2026 - first time since 1972 with no binding U.S.-Russian limits. Oct 2025 directive to begin nuclear testing 'on an equal basis' (implementation unclear).

Chemical stockpile destroyed (7 Jul 2023) - chemical option gone. U.S. destructive DA-ASAT test moratorium (Apr 2022). Space Force (20 Dec 2019); Counter Communications System (2020), Meadowlands jammers (2025-26).

Strikes: Syria (Apr 2017, Apr 2018), MOAB (Apr 2017), Soleimani (Jan 2020), Houthis (2024-25), Midnight Hammer on Iranian nuclear sites (22 Jun 2025), maritime strikes on alleged drug boats (from Sept 2025), Venezuela raid and capture of Maduro (3 Jan 2026), Operation Epic Fury vs Iran with Israel (from 28 Feb 2026, ~5-6 weeks, followed by ceasefire; status after Apr 2026 UNCERTAIN).

Post-INF ground-launched missiles return: Typhon (Philippines 2024), PrSM (2023); Dark Eagle hypersonic battery receiving operational missiles (2026). F-35 fleet; B-21 flight testing, first to Ellsworth 2027.
Economic: sweeping Russia sanctions (2022), export controls on chips to China (2022-), broad tariff actions (2025).

eras.name: Near future (announced, fielded or near-fielded only)
key_facts: Likely by 2030: B-21 Raider in service at Ellsworth (first aircraft 2027); additional Dark Eagle batteries; Conventional Prompt Strike on USS Zumwalt; Collaborative Combat Aircraft (drone wingmen) initial fielding; Virginia Block V with payload module.

Probably NOT by 2030 (flag): Sentinel ICBM (restructured 2024, schedule slipped into the 2030s); Columbia SSBN first patrol (planned ~2030-31, at risk); LRSO (~2030, uncertain); SLCM-N (mid-2030s); F-47 NGAD (first flight targeted 2028).
Treaty environment: no U.S.-Russia strategic limits unless a successor is negotiated; China (~600+ warheads, DoD estimate, growing) not party to any limits.
Chemical: none (destroyed). Biological: none (BWC). Both only as 'restart a banned program' options.

options.name: Infantry (regulars, militia, volunteers, National Guard)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Regular Army + state militia (War of 1812, Mexican War)
options.scale_note: 1789: ~700-840 regulars authorized. War of 1812: regular army authorized ~35,000 (actual peak ~38,000) plus militia. Mexican War: ~100,000 served. Union Army: ~1 million under arms at peak (1865), ~2.1M served. 1866-97: ~25,000 regulars (statutory cap 1876). 1898: ~275,000 incl. volunteers. WWI: ~4 million mobilized, ~2 million sent to France. WWII: Army+AAF ~8.3 million peak, 16 million served in all services. Korea ~330,000 peak in theater (approx). Vietnam 543,400 peak in-country (Apr 1969). Gulf War ~540,000 deployed. Iraq ~170,000 peak (2007), Afghanistan ~100,000 (2010-11). Active Army today ~450,000 (approx).
options.historical_use: Every major U.S. war from the Northwest Indian War (1785-95) onward.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Low for defense or with allies/UN mandate; high for invasion of a sovereign state without authorization (post-1945 UN Charter era).

options.name: Horse cavalry / dragoons

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: A few hundred to a few regiments pre-1861; Union cavalry tens of thousands; 10 regular cavalry regiments in the late 19th c.
options.historical_use: Indian Wars, Mexican War, Civil War, Punitive Expedition 1916. Last U.S. mounted cavalry charge: 26th Cavalry at Morong, Philippines, 16 Jan 1942; remaining horse units dismounted/converted 1942-43.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Same as land forces generally.

options.name: Field and siege artillery (later rocket artillery)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: From a battalion of artillery (1789) to thousands of tubes in WWII; today ~hundreds of HIMARS/MLRS launchers.
options.historical_use: All wars; HIMARS supplied to Ukraine 2022 (by U.S. as aid, not U.S. use).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Standard conventional option.

options.name: Marine Corps / amphibious landing forces

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Marine Expeditionary Units (MEUs) on amphibious ready groups
options.scale_note: ~a few hundred (1800) to 485,000 Marines (1945); today ~170,000 active Marines; 31 amphibious warships (approx).
options.historical_use: Barbary Wars, Mexican War, Banana Wars 1898-1934, WWII Pacific, Korea, Vietnam, Gulf, Iraq. Large-scale amphibious doctrine dates from the 1934 Tentative Manual for Landing Operations.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: MEU presence offshore is a classic signaling tool; landings are acts of war.

options.name: Armor (tanks, mechanized infantry)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: U.S. Tank Corps with Renault FT (1918)
options.scale_note: WWII: 16 armored divisions; Cold War: thousands of tanks in Europe; today ~2,500 M1 Abrams in active/Guard inventory (approx).
options.historical_use: WWI (Saint-Mihiel/Meuse-Argonne, Sept-Nov 1918), WWII, Korea, Gulf War (1991), Iraq (2003).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Heavy armor deployment is a strong escalation/commitment signal.

options.name: Airborne and air-assault forces

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: WWII: 5 airborne divisions; today 82nd Airborne (~18,000) plus 101st (air assault) and 173rd/11th Airborne.
options.historical_use: North Africa/Sicily 1942-43, D-Day 1944, Market Garden 1944, Corregidor 1945, Vietnam (Junction City 1967), Grenada 1983, Panama 1989, Iraq 2003.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Rapid-reaction deployment (82nd's ~18-hour alert brigade) signals resolve.

options.name: Special operations forces

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Thousands in WWII; ~70,000 personnel under USSOCOM today (approx).
options.historical_use: WWII raids, Vietnam, Desert One (Iran, 1980 - failed), Panama 1989, Afghanistan 2001, bin Laden raid (May 2011), Delta Force capture of Maduro in Caracas (3 Jan 2026).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Lower visibility but raids on sovereign territory without consent carry high cost if exposed; deniability is limited.

options.name: Helicopters (assault, attack, medevac)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Sikorsky R-4 (first combat rescue, Burma, Apr 1944)
options.scale_note: Vietnam: ~12,000 helicopters served in theater over the war (approx.); today several thousand across services.
options.historical_use: Korea (medevac/lift), Vietnam (airmobile war), Gulf War, Iraq, Afghanistan.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Standard conventional option.

options.name: No navy - Revenue cutters only

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Continental Navy disbanded 1785 (last ship sold). Between 1785 and 1797 the U.S. had no seagoing warships; Naval Act of 1794 funded six frigates, first launched 1797.
options.historical_use: Customs enforcement only. GAME NOTE: a 1789-1797 President has essentially no naval attack option.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: N/A

options.name: Sailing frigates, sloops and brigs

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Quasi-War 1798-1800: ~50 vessels incl. converted merchantmen. War of 1812: ~17 seagoing warships vs Royal Navy ~600+ (approx). Sail remained primary until 1850s-60s.
options.historical_use: Quasi-War with France (1798-1800), First Barbary War (1801-05), War of 1812 (single-ship victories; Lake Erie 1813, Lake Champlain 1814), Second Barbary War (1815), anti-piracy and anti-slave-trade patrols.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Commerce raiding was standard and accepted.

options.name: Ships of the line

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Congress authorized 9 (Act of 1816); fewer than 10 ever commissioned, most spent years laid up 'in ordinary'.
options.historical_use: Served mainly as squadron flagships and receiving ships; NO U.S. ship of the line ever fought a fleet battle. Several burned at Norfolk Navy Yard in April 1861.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Presence/prestige only.

options.name: Jeffersonian gunboat navy (coastal gunboats)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: ~176 boats, one or two guns each.
options.historical_use: Coastal/harbor defense, Embargo enforcement, War of 1812 (Lake Borgne 1814). Generally judged ineffective.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Defensive posture.

options.name: Privateers / letters of marque

legal_status_by_period.note: Constitution Art. I s.8 gives Congress the power to grant letters of marque.
Declaration of Paris (1856) abolished privateering; the U.S. never signed it, but the practice is obsolete and would be treated as a norm violation.

options.scale_note: War of 1812: privateers took on the order of 1,300+ British merchant prizes (estimates vary widely - UNCERTAIN).
options.historical_use: Quasi-War, War of 1812 (last U.S. use). Confederacy issued letters of marque in 1861 (not U.S.).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Pre-1856 normal; post-1856 high novelty/norm cost; requires an act of Congress.

options.name: Steam warships and ironclads / monitors

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Union Navy grew from ~42 commissioned ships (1861) to ~670 vessels (1865), incl. ~60+ ironclads/monitors (approx). Postwar decline to a few dozen mostly obsolete ships by 1880.
options.historical_use: Hampton Roads (9 Mar 1862, Monitor vs CSS Virginia), Mississippi campaign, Mobile Bay (1864). Old monitors were used for harbor defense in 1898.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Standard.

options.name: Naval blockade / quarantine

legal_status_by_period.note: A belligerent right under customary law (Declaration of Paris 1856: blockades must be effective).
A blockade is an act of war; lawful as self-defense or with UN Security Council authorization. 1962 Cuba action was styled 'quarantine' to avoid the term.

example_systems: WWI/WWII blockades and unrestricted submarine war vs Japan (from 7 Dec 1941)
options.scale_note: Union blockade: ~500 ships along 3,500 miles of coast (approx).
options.historical_use: See examples.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: High; neutral shipping states object. Post-1945 requires a self-defense or UNSC rationale.

options.name: Naval mine warfare

legal_status_by_period.note: Hague Convention VIII (1907) restricts unanchored and automatic contact mines.

example_systems: Civil War 'torpedoes' (mostly Confederate; Union used some)
North Sea Mine Barrage (1918, ~56,000 U.S. mines)
options.scale_note: See examples.
options.historical_use: WWI, WWII, Vietnam (1972), Nicaragua harbor mining by CIA (1984; World Court ruled against U.S. 1986).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Mining a neutral's harbor in peacetime is unlawful (Nicaragua v. U.S., ICJ 1986).

options.name: Steel 'New Navy' cruisers and gunboats

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: 'ABCD' ships: USS Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Dolphin (authorized 1883)
Armored cruisers USS New York, Brooklyn
options.scale_note: A handful of protected cruisers by 1890; ~a dozen armored/protected cruisers by 1898.
options.historical_use: Manila Bay (1 May 1898), Santiago (3 Jul 1898), Boxer Rebellion, Banana Wars gunboat diplomacy.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Gunboat diplomacy era: little cost against weak states, high against European powers.

options.name: Battleships (pre-dreadnought to Iowa class)

legal_status_by_period.note: Washington Naval Treaty (1922) / London (1930): capital-ship tonnage ratio 5:5:3 (US:UK:Japan), building holiday.

example_systems: USS Michigan / South Carolina - first U.S. dreadnoughts (commissioned 1910)
North Carolina, South Dakota, Iowa classes (1941-44)
options.scale_note: 1898: 4 first-class + 1 second-class battleship. 1922 treaty: ~18 U.S. battleships retained. WWII peak: 23-25 battleships (approx). Last active: USS Missouri decommissioned 31 Mar 1992.
options.historical_use: Spanish-American War, WWI (Battleship Division Nine with British Grand Fleet), WWII Pacific/Atlantic shore bombardment and Surigao Strait (Oct 1944), Korea, Vietnam (USS New Jersey 1968-69), Lebanon (1983-84), Gulf War (1991).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Prestige asset; exceeding treaty limits 1922-36 would breach the Washington/London treaties.

options.name: Attack submarines (diesel, later nuclear SSN)

legal_status_by_period.note: Unrestricted submarine warfare by Germany was a U.S. casus belli in 1917.
London Submarine Protocol (1936): subs must follow cruiser rules against merchant ships; U.S. nevertheless declared unrestricted submarine warfare against Japan on 7 Dec 1941.

options.scale_note: WWII: ~288 subs, sank ~55% of Japanese merchant tonnage (approx.); today ~50 SSNs (approx).
options.historical_use: WWI (minor), WWII Pacific (decisive anti-shipping), Cold War ISR, Tomahawk strikes (1991+).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Sinking merchant ships without warning carries high cost with neutrals.

options.name: Aircraft carriers / carrier strike groups

legal_status_by_period.note: Washington Treaty capped U.S. carrier tonnage at 135,000 tons.

example_systems: USS Enterprise CVN-65 (1961, first nuclear carrier)
options.scale_note: 1941: 7 fleet carriers. Aug 1945: ~28 fleet/light + ~70 escort carriers. Cold War: 12-15 carriers. Today: 11 nuclear carriers (statutory minimum).
options.historical_use: Coral Sea and Midway (1942), WWII Pacific, Korea, Vietnam (Yankee Station), Libya 1986, Gulf War, Afghanistan 2001, Iraq, anti-Houthi ops 2023-25, Iran 2025-26.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Carrier deployment is a primary signaling/escalation lever; cost low until used.

options.name: Ballistic missile submarines (SSBN)

legal_status_by_period.note: SALT I (SLBM launcher freeze ~710 / 44 boats), START I, New START launcher/warhead limits.
New START expired 5 Feb 2026; NPT Art. VI disarmament obligation remains; no numerical cap.

example_systems: USS George Washington - first deterrent patrol 15 Nov 1960
Columbia class (first boat expected late 2020s; first patrol ~2030-31 - UNCERTAIN, likely after 2030)
options.scale_note: 41 SSBNs by 1967; 14 Ohio SSBNs today carrying roughly 70% of deployed U.S. strategic warheads (approx).
options.historical_use: Deterrent patrols only; never fired in anger.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Use = nuclear war.

options.name: Cruise-missile submarines (SSGN)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: 4 Ohio SSGNs (retiring ~2026-2028, approx).
options.historical_use: SSGN Tomahawk strikes on Libya (USS Florida, 2011).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Standard conventional strike.

options.name: Observation balloons

legal_status_by_period.note: Hague Declaration (1899) banned discharge of projectiles from balloons for 5 years; renewed 1907 (U.S. ratified the 1907 declaration). Observation was lawful.

example_systems: Signal Corps balloon at San Juan Hill (1898)
options.scale_note: Union: 7 balloons (approx); AEF: ~35 balloon companies at front by Nov 1918 (approx).
options.historical_use: Reconnaissance/artillery spotting only; Balloon Corps disbanded Aug 1863.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: None.

options.name: Military aircraft: fighters and attack/close support

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: AEF Air Service: SPAD XIII, DH-4 (1918)
options.scale_note: Nov 1918: ~45 AEF squadrons, ~740 aircraft at the front (approx). WWII: AAF ~79,000 aircraft (1944 peak, approx). Today: ~several thousand combat aircraft across USAF/USN/USMC.
options.historical_use: Every war from WWI on.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Air strikes are the default 'limited' coercive option post-1945; cost scales with civilian casualties and sovereignty violation.

options.name: Strategic bombers

legal_status_by_period.note: No treaty banned area bombing in WWII; Roosevelt's 1939 appeal against bombing civilians was a policy statement only.
Additional Protocol I (1977) codifies distinction/proportionality; U.S. not party but accepts much as custom. Bombers count under SALT II/START/New START.

example_systems: B-21 Raider (first to Ellsworth AFB in 2027; IOC date not public)
options.scale_note: WWII: thousands of heavy bombers. SAC late 1950s: ~1,800-2,000 bombers incl. ~1,300+ B-47s (approx). Today: ~76 B-52H, ~45 B-1B, ~19-20 B-2A (approx).
options.historical_use: Strategic bombing of Germany and Japan (incl. Tokyo firebombing 9-10 Mar 1945), Korea, Vietnam (Arc Light, Linebacker II Dec 1972), Gulf War, Kosovo (B-2 combat debut 1999), Afghanistan, Iraq, Midnight Hammer (B-2s with GBU-57s on Fordow/Natanz, 22 Jun 2025), Epic Fury (Iran, from 28 Feb 2026).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Bomber deployments are a visible escalation signal; use against cities carries extreme norm cost post-1945.

options.name: Precision-guided munitions

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Paveway laser-guided bombs (Thanh Hoa Bridge, May 1972)
GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator (first combat use Jun 2025)
options.scale_note: Gulf War: ~8% of munitions dropped were guided; by Iraq 2003 ~two-thirds (approx).
options.historical_use: WWII (limited), Vietnam, every conflict since 1991.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Lowers civilian-casualty cost per strike.

options.name: Stealth aircraft

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: 59 F-117As built; 21 B-2s built.
options.historical_use: Panama 1989, Gulf War 1991, Kosovo 1999 (one F-117 lost), Iraq 2003, Iran 2025-26.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Enables strikes with low risk of U.S. losses.

options.name: Drones / UAVs (reconnaissance, then armed)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Armed MQ-1 (first strikes Afghanistan Oct 2001; Yemen Nov 2002)
Collaborative Combat Aircraft YFQ-42A/YFQ-44A (first flights 2025; fielding ~2029-30, UNCERTAIN)
options.scale_note: Hundreds of MQ-1/MQ-9; ~14,000 drone strikes in Pakistan/Yemen/Somalia/Afghanistan 2004-2020 by independent counts (Bureau of Investigative Journalism; approx).
options.historical_use: Targeted killing campaigns (Pakistan from 2004), Iraq/Syria vs ISIS, Soleimani strike (3 Jan 2020), Caribbean/Pacific strikes on alleged drug boats (from Sept 2025).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Low U.S. risk; persistent legal controversy over strikes outside declared war zones.

options.name: Early cruise missiles (nuclear-armed, 1950s-70s)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

options.scale_note: Snark: one squadron; Hound Dog: ~600 built (approx).
options.historical_use: Deterrence only.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Nuclear.

options.name: ICBMs

legal_status_by_period.note: SALT I froze U.S. ICBM launchers at 1,054; START I/New START numerical limits.
No numerical treaty cap after 5 Feb 2026; NPT obligations remain.

example_systems: SM-65 Atlas (first on alert Sept 1959; retired 1965)
Minuteman III (1970, first MIRV ICBM; 400 deployed today)
LGM-35 Sentinel (restructured after 2024 Nunn-McCurdy breach; NOT expected deployed by 2030)
options.scale_note: 1,054 ICBMs (1,000 Minuteman + 54 Titan II) from 1967; 400 single-warhead Minuteman III today.
options.historical_use: Never used in combat.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Use = general nuclear war. Test launches are routine and pre-notified.

options.name: SLBMs

legal_status_by_period.note: SALT I / START / New START limits.
No numerical cap after New START.

example_systems: Trident II D5 (1990-today; D5LE2 planned for Columbia)
options.scale_note: Today ~970 warheads on SLBMs (FAS estimate, Jan 2025).
options.historical_use: Never used in combat.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Nuclear.

options.name: Theater/intermediate-range ballistic missiles

legal_status_by_period.note: INF Treaty banned U.S./Soviet ground-launched missiles 500-5,500 km; U.S. eliminated 846 by 1991.
U.S. withdrew from INF on 2 Aug 2019.

example_systems: PGM-19 Jupiter (Italy, Turkey 1961-63; withdrawn after Cuban crisis)
options.scale_note: Pershing II: 108 launchers in W. Germany.
options.historical_use: Deterrence only. Jupiter withdrawal from Turkey was the secret quid pro quo of the 1962 crisis.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Forward deployment near Russia/China provokes strong reaction (1983 Euromissile crisis; 2024 Typhon protests by China).

options.name: Modern cruise missiles (conventional and nuclear)

legal_status_by_period.note: INF banned ground-launched cruise missiles (BGM-109G GLCM eliminated by 1991); sea/air-launched allowed.

example_systems: AGM-181 LRSO nuclear cruise missile (planned ~2030, UNCERTAIN)
options.scale_note: ~2,000+ Tomahawks fired in combat since 1991 (approx).
options.historical_use: Gulf War (~288 TLAMs), Iraq 1993/1996/1998, Sudan/Afghanistan (Aug 1998), Kosovo, Afghanistan 2001, Iraq 2003 (~800), Libya 2011, Syria (Shayrat Apr 2017: 59; Apr 2018), Houthis 2024-25, Iran 2025-26.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Standard 'punitive strike' option of the 1990s+; low U.S. risk.

options.name: Hypersonic boost-glide weapons (conventional)

legal_status_by_period.note: Subject only to the law of war (Hague 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949, UN Charter 1945 jus ad bellum).

example_systems: Army LRHW 'Dark Eagle' (battery equipment 2021; missed FY2023 goal; successful tests Jun & Dec 2024, Mar 2026; first operational missiles to the JBLM battery 'soon' per Army, Mar 2026)
Navy Conventional Prompt Strike on USS Zumwalt (~2027+) and Virginia Block V (~2028+)
options.scale_note: One battery = 4 launchers, 8 missiles. Expect 1-3 batteries by 2030 (projection, UNCERTAIN).
options.historical_use: None.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Ambiguity (conventional vs nuclear) creates escalation risk with Russia/China.

options.name: Nuclear weapons - strategic strike

legal_status_by_period.note: No treaty restricted possession or use.
NPT (in force 5 Mar 1970) recognizes U.S. as a nuclear-weapon state with Art. VI obligations; SALT I (1972), START I (1994-2009), SORT (2003-11), New START (2011-26) caps.

New START expired 5 Feb 2026 with no successor; Russia offered to observe limits if U.S. reciprocates, Trump sought a 'new, improved' treaty. No binding numerical cap as of late 2026 (verify for current status).

example_systems: B61, B83 bombs; W76, W78, W87, W88 warheads
options.scale_note: Stockpile (NNSA/DOE, end of FY; excludes retired awaiting dismantlement): 1945: 2 | 1950: 299 | 1955: 2,422 | 1960: 18,638 | 1962: 25,540 | 1967 peak: 31,255 | 1975: 27,519 | 1980: 24,104 | 1989: 22,217 | 1991: 19,008 | 1995: 10,904 | 2001: 10,526 | 2005: 8,360 | 2010: 5,066 | 2015: 4,571 | 2020: 3,750 | 2023: 3,748. FAS Jan 2025: ~3,700 stockpile, ~1,770 deployed (400 ICBM, ~970 SLBM, ~300 bomber bases, ~100 in Europe), ~1,477 retired awaiting dismantlement. Pre-1962 figures from the 1993 DOE release.
options.historical_use: Hiroshima (6 Aug 1945) and Nagasaki (9 Aug 1945) - the only combat use ever. Considered/threatened in Korea (1950-53), Taiwan Strait (1954-55, 1958), Berlin, Cuba 1962 (DEFCON 2), 1973 (DEFCON 3).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Catastrophic: first use since 1945 would break the 'nuclear taboo'; expect allied rupture, global condemnation, retaliation risk from 1949 (USSR test) onward and assured destruction from the mid-1960s.

options.name: Nuclear weapons - tactical / non-strategic

legal_status_by_period.note: 1991 Presidential Nuclear Initiatives withdrew Army ground-launched and most naval tactical nukes; only B61 bombs (~100 in Europe, NATO nuclear sharing) remain. Not covered by any treaty.

options.scale_note: Peak ~7,000 U.S. tactical warheads in Europe (early 1970s, approx); non-strategic weapons down >90% since 1991 (NNSA).
options.historical_use: None in combat.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Same nuclear taboo; 'limited' use risks escalation to strategic exchange.

options.name: Nuclear test (signaling option)

legal_status_by_period.note: Atmospheric testing 1945-62 (Nevada, Pacific; Castle Bravo 1954).
Limited Test Ban Treaty (1963) bans atmospheric, underwater, space tests; Threshold Test Ban (signed 1974, in force 1990) caps at 150 kt.

Unilateral moratorium since Oct 1992 (last test 'Divider', 23 Sept 1992); CTBT signed 1996, Senate rejected 1999. Oct 2025 presidential directive to begin testing 'on an equal basis' - implementation unclear (UNCERTAIN). Underground test would require months to ~3 years of preparation per public NNSA statements (approx).

options.scale_note: 1,054 U.S. tests 1945-1992 (DOE count).
options.historical_use: Signaling throughout the Cold War.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Post-1992: high; would likely trigger Russian/Chinese resumption and NPT backlash.

options.name: Chemical weapons

legal_status_by_period.note: Not stockpiled. U.S. declined to sign the 1899 Hague Declaration on asphyxiating gas projectiles (Mahan). 1907 Hague IV bans 'poison or poisoned weapons'. Not a practical option.
Used in WWI after Germany's 1915 first use: AEF Gas Service (Aug 1917), 1st Gas Regiment, Chemical Warfare Service created 28 Jun 1918; Edgewood Arsenal production.

Geneva Protocol signed 1925 but NOT ratified by U.S. until 1975. FDR's June 1943 no-first-use pledge; large WWII stockpile, never used in combat. Sarin produced 1950s, VX 1960s. Nixon Nov 1969 renounced first use of lethal/incapacitating agents. Herbicides (Agent Orange, 1962-71) and riot-control agents used in Vietnam - contested under the Protocol.

Geneva Protocol ratified 22 Jan 1975 (bans first use; U.S. reserved retaliation). Possession legal. Binary munitions produced 1987-1990. 1990 U.S.-USSR destruction agreement; May 1991 Bush forswore use for any reason including retaliation.
CWC in force 29 Apr 1997 (U.S. ratified 25 Apr 1997): use, production, stockpiling banned; stockpile under verified destruction.
Last U.S. declared chemical munition (sarin M55 rocket) destroyed 7 Jul 2023 at Blue Grass, KY; OPCW verified. Option no longer exists.

options.scale_note: Declared stockpile ~30,000 metric tons of agent (OPCW/ACA, 'nearly 30,000'); ~90% destroyed by 2012 at earlier sites, final ~10% at Pueblo (done Jun 2023) and Blue Grass (7 Jul 2023).
options.historical_use: WWI only (1918). Not used in WWII, Korea, or later (except herbicides/riot-control agents in Vietnam, which the U.S. maintained were not chemical weapons).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Pre-1925 moderate; 1925-1997 severe norm violation; post-1997 not available. GAME: model as 'restart a banned program' requiring CWC withdrawal (90-day notice, Art. XVI) and multi-year rebuild (designer estimate, not a public figure).

options.name: Biological weapons

legal_status_by_period.note: No U.S. program; not a practical option.
Offensive program at Camp (later Fort) Detrick from 1943; production at Pine Bluff Arsenal from 1954; Geneva Protocol not ratified by U.S. Agents standardized but never used in war.
Nixon renounced all biological warfare 25 Nov 1969 (toxins added Feb 1970); stockpile destroyed 1971-73.
BWC signed 10 Apr 1972, ratified and in force for U.S. 26 Mar 1975. Defensive research only. No U.S. stockpile since the early 1970s.

options.scale_note: Small stockpile of standardized agents (details beyond scope).
options.historical_use: Never used in combat.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Post-1975: 'restart a banned program' - requires BWC withdrawal (3-month notice, Art. XIII) or covert violation; designer suggestion: multi-year lead time and extreme diplomatic/domestic cost. The U.S. does NOT have bioweapons today.

options.name: Offensive cyber operations

legal_status_by_period.note: No treaty; UN GGE norms (2015) and the non-binding Tallinn Manual apply international law. NSPM-13 (2018) eased presidential approval.

example_systems: 'Olympic Games'/Stuxnet vs Iran's Natanz (from ~2007-08; discovered 2010; attributed to U.S./Israel by press, never officially acknowledged - UNCERTAIN)
USCYBERCOM (IOC 21 May 2010, FOC Oct 2010; unified combatant command May 2018)
Disruption of Russia's IRA during 2018 midterms
options.scale_note: 133 Cyber Mission Force teams (~6,200 personnel; full operational capability 2018).
options.historical_use: See examples.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Usually deniable; attacks on civilian infrastructure (power grid) carry high escalation cost and invite retaliation.

options.name: Anti-satellite (ASAT) / counter-space

legal_status_by_period.note: Outer Space Treaty (1967) bans nuclear weapons in orbit and on celestial bodies; ASAT not banned. Congress barred ASAT tests against objects in space 1985-88.
U.S. unilateral moratorium on destructive direct-ascent ASAT missile tests (announced 18 Apr 2022); non-destructive counter-space (jamming) fielded.

example_systems: Program 505 Nike Zeus nuclear ASAT, Kwajalein (1963-66)
Program 437 Thor nuclear ASAT, Johnston Island (1964-75)
ASM-135 from F-15 destroys Solwind satellite (13 Sept 1985)
Operation Burnt Frost - SM-3 destroys USA-193 (21 Feb 2008)
options.scale_note: A handful of operational launchers at any time; today ~a dozen-plus mobile jammers planned (Meadowlands target 32, approx).
options.historical_use: Tests only; no combat ASAT use.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Destructive debris-producing ASAT tests now draw broad condemnation (UNGA 2022 resolution).

options.name: U.S. Space Force operations

legal_status_by_period.note: Outer Space Treaty constraints.

options.scale_note: ~10,000 Guardians (approx).
options.historical_use: Support to operations (e.g., Midnight Hammer cited by USSF).
options.diplomatic_cost_note: See ASAT.

options.name: Embargo, trade war, financial sanctions

legal_status_by_period.note: Domestic authority: Embargo Act (Dec 1807), Non-Intercourse Act (1809), Trading with the Enemy Act (6 Oct 1917), OFAC (Dec 1950), IEEPA (1977). Unilateral sanctions raise WTO/third-party objections.

example_systems: Export controls and asset freeze vs Japan (Jul 1940-Aug 1941 oil embargo)
options.scale_note: Dollar dominance makes post-1945 financial sanctions the most-used U.S. coercive tool.
options.historical_use: See examples. Jefferson's 1807 embargo hurt the U.S. more than Britain; the 1941 oil embargo precipitated Pearl Harbor.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Low-to-moderate; allies resent secondary sanctions; overuse erodes dollar leverage (game: diminishing returns).

options.name: Covert action - early equivalents

legal_status_by_period.note: Contingent Fund of Foreign Intercourse (1790) let presidents spend secretly.

options.scale_note: Ad hoc agents; tiny budgets.
options.historical_use: Barbary regime-change attempt (1805), Civil War espionage, Banana Wars intrigue.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Low if not exposed.

options.name: Covert action - OSS / CIA

legal_status_by_period.note: OSS 13 Jun 1942-1 Oct 1945; National Security Act (26 Jul 1947) created CIA (18 Sept 1947); NSC 10/2 (Jun 1948) authorized covert operations.

Hughes-Ryan (1974) requires presidential findings; Church Committee (1975); EO 11905 (1976) and EO 12333 (1981) ban assassination; Intelligence Oversight Act (1980) requires congressional notification.

example_systems: Post-9/11 CIA paramilitary/drone program (Sept 2001 Memorandum of Notification)
options.scale_note: OSS ~13,000 personnel at peak.
options.historical_use: See examples.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Moderate-to-severe when exposed (Bay of Pigs, Iran-Contra 1986); domestic political cost after 1975.

options.name: Restart a chemical weapons program (banned)

legal_status_by_period.note: Requires withdrawal from the CWC (90 days' notice, Art. XVI) or covert violation.

options.scale_note: No stockpile exists. Game suggestion: multi-year lead time before any usable capability; this is a designer estimate, not a published figure.
options.historical_use: None.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Extreme: pariah status, OPCW referral, allied rupture, domestic opposition (Congress funds would be required).

options.name: Restart a biological weapons program (banned)

legal_status_by_period.note: Requires BWC withdrawal (3 months' notice, Art. XIII) or covert violation.

options.scale_note: No stockpile since the early 1970s. Game suggestion: multi-year lead time; designer estimate only.
options.historical_use: None.
options.diplomatic_cost_note: Extreme; arguably worse than chemical. Should be near-impossible to approve domestically.

fleets.name: Mediterranean Squadron
fleets.home_region: Mediterranean (Barbary coast; bases at Gibraltar, Port Mahon, La Spezia)
fleets.notes: Ad hoc squadrons sent 1801-07 for the First Barbary War; permanent station from 1815 (Decatur, Second Barbary War). Recalled 1861 for the Civil War; reconstituted as the European Squadron 1865.

fleets.name: West India Squadron
fleets.notes: Anti-piracy (David Porter). Merged into the Home Squadron 1842.

fleets.name: Pacific Squadron
fleets.home_region: Pacific coast of the Americas (Valparaiso, Callao; later San Francisco)
fleets.notes: Seized California ports in the Mexican War (1846). Became part of the Pacific Fleet 1907.

fleets.name: Brazil Squadron / South Atlantic Squadron
fleets.notes: Brazil Squadron 1826-1861; South Atlantic Squadron 1865-1905.

fleets.name: East India Squadron
fleets.home_region: East Asia / Indian Ocean (Canton, Hong Kong)
fleets.notes: Perry's 'Black Ships' expedition to Japan (1853-54) operated from it. Became the Asiatic Squadron 1868.

fleets.name: Home Squadron
fleets.home_region: U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts, Caribbean
fleets.notes: Gulf blockade and Veracruz landing (1847). Replaced by blockading squadrons in 1861.

fleets.name: Africa Squadron
fleets.notes: Anti-slave-trade patrols under the Webster-Ashburton Treaty (1842).

fleets.name: Union Blockading Squadrons (North Atlantic, South Atlantic, East Gulf, West Gulf) and Mississippi River Squadron
fleets.notes: Atlantic and Gulf blockading squadrons were split into North/South and East/West in late 1861-early 1862. Farragut's West Gulf squadron took New Orleans (Apr 1862) and Mobile Bay (Aug 1864).

fleets.name: European Squadron
fleets.notes: Successor to the Mediterranean Squadron.

fleets.name: North Atlantic Squadron
fleets.notes: Sampson's squadron destroyed Cervera's fleet at Santiago (3 Jul 1898). Became the North Atlantic Fleet 1902, then the Atlantic Fleet.

fleets.name: Asiatic Squadron / Asiatic Fleet
fleets.notes: Dewey's Asiatic Squadron won at Manila Bay (1 May 1898). Upgraded to Asiatic Fleet 1902; dissolved Feb 1942 after defeat in the Dutch East Indies. Included the Yangtze Patrol (1854/1921-1941).

fleets.name: Flying Squadron
fleets.notes: Commodore Schley's fast squadron held at Hampton Roads against feared Spanish raids, then sent to Cuba.

fleets.name: Atlantic Fleet
fleets.notes: Formed from the North Atlantic Fleet (c. 1905-06, date approx.). Its battleships made up the Great White Fleet. Merged into U.S. Fleet 1922; re-created 1 Feb 1941.

fleets.name: Great White Fleet
fleets.home_region: World cruise (Hampton Roads to Hampton Roads)
fleets.notes: 16 battleships, ~14,000 sailors, 16 Dec 1907 - 22 Feb 1909; Roosevelt's demonstration of U.S. naval power (notably to Japan).

fleets.name: Pacific Fleet (first)
fleets.notes: Merged into U.S. Fleet 1922.

fleets.name: United States Fleet (Battle Fleet / Scouting Fleet)
fleets.home_region: Battle Fleet in the Pacific (San Pedro; to Pearl Harbor 1940); Scouting Fleet in the Atlantic (to 1932)
fleets.notes: Single fleet organization under the Washington Treaty era; split again into Atlantic, Pacific and Asiatic Fleets 1 Feb 1941.

fleets.name: U.S. Pacific Fleet
fleets.notes: Parent of 3rd and 7th Fleets today.

fleets.name: U.S. Atlantic Fleet / U.S. Fleet Forces Command
fleets.notes: Renamed U.S. Fleet Forces Command 2006.

fleets.name: First Fleet
fleets.notes: Disestablished 1973 (functions to 3rd Fleet). Re-establishment proposed 2020 but not done (as of 2025).

fleets.name: Second Fleet
fleets.notes: Second Task Fleet 1947, Second Fleet 1950; disestablished 2011, re-established 2018 vs Russian naval activity.

fleets.name: Third Fleet
fleets.notes: Halsey's WWII fleet (alternated with 5th Fleet staff over the same ships); inactive 1945-73, re-established 1973.

fleets.name: Fourth Fleet
fleets.home_region: South Atlantic (WWII); Caribbean, Central & South America (2008-)
fleets.notes: Disestablished 1950; re-established Jul 2008 (Mayport). Gap 1950-2008.

fleets.name: Fifth Fleet
fleets.notes: Spruance's WWII fleet; inactive c.1947-1995; re-established Jul 1995 for the Gulf. Gap c.1947-1995.

fleets.name: Sixth Fleet
fleets.notes: Naval Forces Mediterranean 1946, Sixth Task Fleet 1948, Sixth Fleet Feb 1950.

fleets.name: Seventh Fleet
fleets.notes: MacArthur's Navy in WWII; Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan Strait patrols. Largest forward-deployed fleet.

fleets.name: Eighth Fleet
fleets.notes: Hewitt's amphibious fleet (Sicily, Salerno, southern France). End date approx.; designation briefly reused 1946-47 for Atlantic.

fleets.name: Tenth Fleet / Fleet Cyber Command
fleets.home_region: WWII: Atlantic ASW coordination (no ships); 2010-: cyber (Fort Meade)
fleets.notes: Disestablished 1945; re-established Jan 2010 as Navy's cyber component. Gap 1945-2010.

fleets.name: Twelfth Fleet
fleets.notes: U.S. Naval Forces Europe in WWII.

treaties.name: Declaration of Paris
treaties.effect: Abolished privateering; U.S. did not sign.

treaties.name: Hague Conventions
treaties.effect: Law of war; 1899 gas-projectile declaration NOT signed by U.S.; 1907 Hague IV 'poison' ban ratified; Hague VIII mines.

treaties.name: Washington / London Naval Treaties
treaties.effect: Capital ship and carrier tonnage caps (US:UK:Japan 5:5:3); Japan left 1936.

treaties.name: Geneva Protocol
treaties.effect: Bans first use of chemical and biological weapons.

treaties.name: Kellogg-Briand Pact
treaties.effect: Renounced war as national policy.

treaties.name: UN Charter
treaties.effect: Bans use of force except self-defense (Art. 51) or UNSC authorization.

treaties.name: Limited Test Ban Treaty
treaties.effect: No atmospheric/space/underwater nuclear tests.

treaties.name: Outer Space Treaty
treaties.effect: No nuclear weapons in orbit.

treaties.name: NPT
treaties.effect: U.S. a recognized nuclear-weapon state; Art. VI disarmament obligation.

treaties.name: SALT I Interim Agreement
treaties.effect: Froze ICBM/SLBM launchers (U.S. 1,054 ICBMs, 710 SLBMs).

treaties.name: ABM Treaty
treaties.effect: U.S. withdrew 13 Jun 2002.

treaties.name: BWC
treaties.effect: Bans biological weapons.

treaties.name: SALT II
treaties.effect: 2,250 launcher cap; U.S. observed until 1986.

treaties.name: INF Treaty
treaties.effect: Banned 500-5,500 km ground-launched missiles; U.S. withdrew 2 Aug 2019.

treaties.name: START I
treaties.effect: 6,000 accountable warheads / 1,600 delivery vehicles.

treaties.name: START II
treaties.effect: 3,000-3,500 warheads; Russia withdrew 2002.

treaties.name: CTBT
treaties.effect: U.S. signed 1996; Senate rejected 1999; U.S. observes test moratorium since 1992.

treaties.name: CWC
treaties.effect: Bans chemical weapons; U.S. stockpile destroyed 7 Jul 2023.

treaties.name: SORT (Moscow Treaty)
treaties.effect: 1,700-2,200 operationally deployed strategic warheads by 2012.

treaties.name: New START
treaties.effect: 1,550 deployed warheads, 700 deployed launchers, 800 total; extended 2021; Russia suspended participation Feb 2023; expired 5 Feb 2026 with no successor.
